Vocab 0009 · Silmulator · from issue #18, commit 58b7e2d
71

ADC Reference Transfer Functions — Vocabulary

72

Eight terms behind the reference-aware ADC conversion. Each has a definition, a project example from the real code, a usage sentence, and a contrast with the term it's most often confused with.

73
74 75
76 reference voltage 77 full-scale code 78 transfer function 79 LSB voltage 80 ADC12VRSEL 81 REF_A 82 VeREF+ 83 ratiometric measurement 84
85 86 87
88

Reference voltage (VR+ / VR−)

89
the conversion's unit of measure
90
91
Definition
92
The voltage pair an ADC compares its input against: VR+ maps to the full-scale code, VR− maps to code 0. Every output code is a fraction of the span between them — the reference literally defines what one "unit" of the result means. Change the reference and the same physical input produces a different code.
93
Project example
94
In silmulator/devices/msp430.py, _adc_reference_voltage() resolves VR+ at conversion time — clock.vcc for AVCC, _veref_v for VEREF, or an ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V lookup for REF_A's outputs. VR− is fixed at AVSS (0 V) in this model. Before commit 58b7e2d, this function didn't exist and VR+ was a hardcoded 3.3.
95
Usage
96
"The RAW code looks huge because you left the 1.2-V reference voltage selected — 1.2 V in, 1.2 V reference, full scale out."
97
Contrast with: supply voltage
98
The supply (AVCC) powers the chip; the reference calibrates the measurement. They coincide only when AVCC is selected as the reference — and then supply drift becomes measurement drift, which is exactly what CPU:VCC 3.0 now lets a SIL test exercise.
99
100
101 102 103
104

Full-scale code (FS)

105
4095 · 1023 · 255
106
107
Definition
108
The maximum code an ADC can output: 2resolution − 1. It is produced when Vin ≥ VR+, so reading it means "at or above the reference" — possibly clipping — never a specific voltage.
109
Project example
110
msp430_faults.py computes max_code = (1 << resolution) - 1 and clamps with max(0, min(max_code, code)). The audit probe adc_ignores_reference asserts that 1.2 V against the 1.2-V VREF returns exactly 4095 — the input equals the reference, so the result is full scale.
111
Usage
112
"Inject 2.5 V against VREF2.0 and you'll read the full-scale code — the ideal 5118 clips to 4095."
113
Contrast with: full-scale voltage
114
The full-scale code is fixed by ADC:RESOLUTION (ADC12RES); the full-scale voltage is whatever reference is selected. Switching VREF2.5 → AVCC moves the voltage that produces 4095 from 2.5 V to 3.3 V, but 4095 itself never changes.
115
116
117 118 119
120

Transfer function

121
SLAU367P §34.2.1, Equation 13
122
123
Definition
124
The mapping from analog input to digital output code: NADC = FS × (Vin − VR−) / (VR+ − VR−), quantised and clamped. It makes explicit that an ADC code is a ratio of the reference span, not a voltage.
125
Project example
126
Implemented in FaultState.adc_code(): int(voltage / full_scale_v * max_code) with VR− = 0. Commit 58b7e2d's whole point was feeding the correct full_scale_v (the selected reference) into this function instead of the literal 3.3 — the CORNER profile then layers gain/offset/INL errors on top of the same ideal transfer curve.
127
Usage
128
"Work the transfer function forward to predict the code, and backward to recover volts — with the same reference both ways, or you get commit-58b7e2d's bug class."
129
Contrast with: calibration curve
130
The transfer function is the ideal, datasheet-defined mapping. A calibration curve characterises how a particular part deviates from it (gain, offset, INL — what the simulator's CORNER fault profile injects). You design against the transfer function; you correct against a calibration.
131
132
133 134 135
136

LSB voltage

137
(VR+ − VR−) / FS
138
139
Definition
140
The input-voltage width of one code step — the smallest voltage change the conversion can resolve. Set jointly by the reference span and the resolution: shrink the reference or raise the resolution, and each code is worth fewer microvolts.
141
Project example
142
With the references Silmulator now honours: 1.2 V / 4095 ≈ 293 µV per LSB under VREF, versus 3.3 V / 4095 ≈ 806 µV under default AVCC. The CORNER profile's INL spec is quoted in these units — a ±2.2-LSB bow in msp430_faults.py — which is only meaningful once you know the LSB's voltage value.
143
Usage
144
"Reading a 0–1 V sensor against AVCC wastes resolution — switch to VREF1.2 and your LSB voltage drops from 806 µV to 293 µV."
145
Contrast with: resolution (bit count)
146
Resolution is the number of steps (12-bit → 4096 of them); LSB voltage is how many volts each step spans. ADC:RESOLUTION changes the step count; ADC:REFERENCE changes the step size. Both knobs move the LSB voltage, only one moves the code range.
147
148
149 150 151
152

ADC12VRSEL

153
SLAU367P §34.2.4 — reference-select register field
154
155
Definition
156
The 4-bit field in the MSP430's ADC12MCTLx conversion-memory registers that selects which physical sources drive VR+ and VR−. Because it is a register field, the set of possible references is finite and fixed by silicon — there is no encoding for an arbitrary voltage.
157
Project example
158
VALID_ADC_REFERENCES = frozenset({"AVCC", "VEREF"} | set(ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V)) in msp430.py mirrors the VRSEL choices the model exposes. ADC:REFERENCE BANANA — or 1.8 — has no encoding, so _adc_ref raises ScpiError(-224, "Illegal ADC reference: …"), matching test_reference_out_of_range_rejected.
159
Usage
160
"The SCPI layer rejects free-form references because ADC12VRSEL is an enum in silicon, not a dial."
161
Contrast with: REFVSEL
162
ADC12VRSEL (in the ADC) picks which source feeds the reference inputs; REFVSEL (in REF_A, §33.3.1) picks which voltage — 1.2/2.0/2.5 V — the internal reference module generates. Silmulator folds both into one token: VREF2.5 effectively sets REFVSEL = 10b and points VRSEL at the internal reference.
163
164
165 166 167
168

REF_A

169
SLAU367P §33 — shared reference module
170
171
Definition
172
The FR5994's on-chip reference generator: a bandgap-derived module shared by the ADC and comparators that outputs a precise, supply-independent 1.2, 2.0, or 2.5 V (selected by REFVSEL, reset default 00b = 1.2 V).
173
Project example
174
Modelled by the ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V dict — {"VREF": 1.2, "VREF1.2": 1.2, "VREF2.0": 2.0, "VREF2.5": 2.5} — with bare VREF deliberately mapped to the REFVSEL reset value. The audit's MISSING list notes what is still absent: REFCTL0 semantics (REFON/REFOUT/REFGENRDY/REFBGRDY bits and the request/ready handshake).
175
Usage
176
"For an absolute battery-voltage reading, don't reference AVCC — take REF_A's 2.5-V output so supply sag can't skew the measurement."
177
Contrast with: AVCC as a reference
178
REF_A's outputs are fixed absolute voltages, immune to supply drift; AVCC tracks the supply (Silmulator reads clock.vcc live). Absolute measurements want REF_A; ratiometric sensors powered from the rail want AVCC.
179
180
181 182 183
184

VeREF+

185
SLASE54D Table 7-1 — external reference pin
186
187
Definition
188
The MSP430 pin through which a board supplies its own external positive reference — typically a precision reference IC (2.048 V, 4.096 V, …). Its voltage is a board-design decision, not a chip property, and it has no defined reset state after BOR.
189
Project example
190
Commit 58b7e2d added self._veref_v (default 1.2, restored by *RST) and the two-parameter SCPI form ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,2.1 — select the pin and declare what the board wires to it. A non-numeric voltage raises ScpiError(-104, …), pinned by test_veref_voltage_param_must_be_numeric.
191
Usage
192
"Our flight board has a 2.048-V reference IC on VeREF+, so the SIL setup sends ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,2.048 before any conversion."
193
Contrast with: VREF (internal)
194
VREF tokens select REF_A's on-chip outputs — fixed at 1.2/2.0/2.5 V, no configuration needed. VeREF+ is off-chip: any voltage the board provides, which is why it is the only reference whose value the test must declare (and the only one with a -104 failure mode).
195
196
197 198 199
200

Ratiometric measurement

201
when the supply cancels out
202
203
Definition
204
A measurement arrangement where the sensor's output and the ADC's reference derive from the same source, so the conversion measures the sensor's fraction and the source's absolute value cancels out of the transfer function: N = FS × (k·AVCC)/AVCC = FS × k.
205
Project example
206
Selecting ADC:REFERENCE AVCC makes _adc_reference_voltage() return self.clock.vcc live. A divider-style sensor modelled by injecting k × vcc reads the same code before and after CPU:VCC 3.0 — while an absolute injection like the fixed 1.2 V shifts from 1489 to 1638, which is how a SIL test tells the two arrangements apart.
207
Usage
208
"The potentiometer is powered from the rail, so keep the conversion ratiometric — referencing it to VREF2.5 would re-introduce the supply drift you're trying to cancel."
209
Contrast with: absolute measurement
210
Absolute measurement answers "how many volts?" and needs a supply-independent reference (REF_A or VeREF+). Ratiometric measurement answers "what fraction of the excitation?" and wants the supply as the reference. Choosing the wrong mode for the sensor type is a real firmware bug class the reference-aware model can now surface.

1. A Clock Signal Is Source × Divider, Not a Stored Number

The single most important idea in this lesson: a system clock has no frequency of its own. MCLK, SMCLK, and ACLK are not oscillators — they are routes. Each one is a multiplexer that picks an oscillator, followed by a divider that scales it. The frequency you observe on the pin is a derived value:

fclock  =  fselected source divider resolve the source → look up its base frequency → apply the divider — every time, at read time

Nothing in the hardware "stores" the number 1 MHz for MCLK. What the CS (Clock System) module stores is configuration: a 3-bit source-select field and a 3-bit divider field per clock. Ask "what is MCLK's frequency?" and the only honest answer walks the tree:

  1. Resolve the source: which oscillator does the mux currently select? (CSCTL2.SELM)
  2. Get the base frequency: what does that oscillator run at right now? (DCO setting × drift, crystal value, or a fixed internal rate)
  3. Apply the divider: divide by the configured /1…/32. (CSCTL3.DIVM)

Skip step 1 — assume the source is always the DCO — and you get a number that is sometimes right (when DCO happens to be selected) and wildly wrong otherwise. That is exactly the bug commit 701853d fixed. With MCLK switched to the 32.768-kHz LFXT crystal, the old model still reported 1 000 000 Hz — off by a factor of ~30.5.

💡 The mental model
Think of a clock as a plumbing route, not a tank. The question "how much water comes out of the MCLK tap?" depends on which reservoir the valve currently points at and how far the restrictor is closed. Caching yesterday's flow rate — or always quoting the DCO reservoir — answers a different question than the one asked.

2. The FR5994 Clock Tree — Sources, Muxes, and Dividers

The MSP430FR5994's CS module (SLAU367P chapter 3) generates three system clocks from six possible oscillators. The routing is set by CSCTL2 (three source-select fields) and CSCTL3 (three divider fields):

ClockMux fieldSelectable sources (SLAU367P §3.3.2)Divider fieldFeeds
MCLKCSCTL2.SELMLFXT, VLO, LFMODCLK, DCO, MODCLK, HFXTCSCTL3.DIVMCPU and system
SMCLKCSCTL2.SELSsame six as MCLKCSCTL3.DIVSTimers, eUSCI (UART/SPI/I2C)
ACLKCSCTL2.SELALFXT, VLO, LFMODCLK onlyCSCTL3.DIVALow-power peripherals, RTC, slow timers

Two structural facts matter:

  • ACLK's mux is narrower. ACLK is the "auxiliary" low-frequency clock, intended to keep ticking in low-power modes — so its mux only offers the three low-frequency sources. CLOCK:ACLK:SOURCE DCO is not a policy choice the simulator makes; there is no SELA encoding for DCO on this silicon.
  • All three dividers share one encoding. DIVM/DIVS/DIVA are 3-bit fields whose defined encodings are /1, /2, /4, /8, /16, /32. There is no /64 and no /128 — values the pre-fix model happily accepted.

What the model stores per clock

# silmulator/devices/msp430.py — ClockState after 701853d
@dataclass
class ClockState:
    mclk_source: str = "DCO"   # DCO | LFXT | HFXT | VLO | MODCLK | LFMODCLK
    mclk_div: int = 1
    smclk_source: str = "DCO"  # same source set as MCLK (CSCTL2.SELS)
    smclk_div: int = 1
    aclk_source: str = "LFXT"  # LFXT | VLO | LFMODCLK (CSCTL2.SELA)
    aclk_div: int = 1
    dco_frequency: float = 1e6  # Hz
    lfxt_frequency: float = 32768.0
    # HFXT has no fixed nominal in hardware — it is an external crystal whose
    # range is configured via CSCTL4.HFFREQ (SLAU367P §3.3.4, not modeled).
    hfxt_frequency: float = 4e6  # simulator-only default
    vcc: float = 3.3

Note what is stored: sources and dividers — configuration — plus base frequencies for the two crystals and the DCO. No per-clock frequency field exists anywhere. That is deliberate: storing mclk_frequency would be a second copy of derivable truth, and the two copies would eventually disagree (the same double-store bug class as the old independent timer period field from lesson 0010's commit family).

⚠ Where is REFO?
If you have used MSP430F5xx/6xx parts, you may reach for REFO — the 32-kHz trimmed reference oscillator in those parts' UCS clock module. The FR59xx CS module does not have it: no SELM/SELS/SELA encoding maps to REFO (same for DCOCLKDIV). The pre-fix model accepted CLOCK:MCLK:SOURCE REFO and rejected MODCLK — exactly backwards for this chip.

3. The Fix — What Commit 701853d Actually Changed

Issue #20 came out of the MSP430 compliance audit. Five clock probes flagged the same theme: the model stored clock configuration but neither validated it against the FR5994's real encodings nor used it when answering frequency queries.

Before: FREQUENCY? hardwired to one oscillator per clock

# silmulator/devices/msp430.py — BEFORE 701853d
def _clk_mclk_freq(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
    freq = self._dco_actual() / self.clock.mclk_div      # ← always DCO
    return f"{freq:.0f}"

def _clk_aclk_freq(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
    freq = self.clock.lfxt_frequency / self.clock.aclk_div # ← always LFXT
    return f"{freq:.0f}"

The source-select commands stored the selection (self.clock.mclk_source = v) but the query never read it back. SMCLK's source and all SMCLK/ACLK dividers were not validated at all (CLOCK:SMCLK:SOURCE BANANA succeeded), MCLK's validation set wrongly contained REFO and DCOCLKDIV, and dividers allowed /64 and /128.

After: one resolver walks the tree

# silmulator/devices/msp430.py — AFTER 701853d
def _clock_source_frequency(self, source: str) -> float:
    """Effective frequency (Hz) of one clock-system source, pre-divider.

    SLAU367P §3.2: DCO is the drift-affected trimmed oscillator
    (``_dco_actual()``); LFXT/HFXT read the crystal fields on
    ``ClockState``; VLO and MODCLK are fixed-frequency internal
    oscillators with no configurable register; LFMODCLK is MODCLK/128.
    """
    if source == "DCO":
        return self._dco_actual()          # dco_frequency × fault-profile drift
    if source == "LFXT":
        return self.clock.lfxt_frequency   # 32768 default
    if source == "HFXT":
        return self.clock.hfxt_frequency   # 4e6 simulator-only default
    if source == "VLO":
        return VLO_FREQUENCY_HZ            # 9400.0 — fixed, no register
    if source == "MODCLK":
        return MODCLK_FREQUENCY_HZ         # 4.8e6 — fixed, no register
    if source == "LFMODCLK":
        return LFMODCLK_FREQUENCY_HZ       # MODCLK / 128 = 37500
    raise ScpiError(-221, f"No simulated frequency for clock source {source}")

def _clk_mclk_freq(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
    freq = self._clock_source_frequency(self.clock.mclk_source) / self.clock.mclk_div
    return f"{freq:.0f}"   # SMCLK and ACLK queries are the same shape

Validation now mirrors the register encodings

# CSCTL2.SELM/SELS: MCLK and SMCLK share one source mux. REFO and DCOCLKDIV
# have no encoding on the FR59xx CS; MODCLK and LFMODCLK do.
VALID_MCLK_SMCLK_SOURCES = frozenset({"LFXT", "VLO", "LFMODCLK", "DCO", "MODCLK", "HFXT"})
# CSCTL2.SELA: ACLK's source mux is a narrower subset of the above.
VALID_ACLK_SOURCES = frozenset({"LFXT", "VLO", "LFMODCLK"})
# CSCTL3.DIVM/DIVS/DIVA: all three dividers share the same 3-bit, power-of-two
# encoding that tops out at /32 (values above /32 have no encoding).
VALID_CLOCK_DIVIDERS = frozenset({1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32})

Every setter now checks its set before storing — a bad source raises ScpiError(-224, "Illegal clock source: …"), a bad divider raises ScpiError(-222, "Illegal divider: …"), and in both cases the previous state is left unchanged. Note the divider error code changed from -224 to -222: a divider is numeric data outside the representable range (-222, "Data out of range"), while a source token outside the enum is an illegal parameter value (-224).

The timer path was fixed the same way

# _timer_tick_frequency — timers now see the real tree, not a hardwired source
if ts.clock_source == "SMCLK":
    src = self._dco_actual() / self.clock.smclk_div
    src = self._clock_source_frequency(self.clock.smclk_source) / self.clock.smclk_div
elif ts.clock_source == "ACLK":
    src = self.clock.lfxt_frequency / self.clock.aclk_div
    src = self._clock_source_frequency(self.clock.aclk_source) / self.clock.aclk_div

Two audit-derived tests dropped their @pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True) decorators, becoming permanent regression guards:

# tests/test_msp430_edge_cases.py — AFTER 701853d (xfail decorators removed)

    # SLAU367P §3.3.3: DIVM encodings stop at /32.
    mcu.process("CLOCK:MCLK:DIVIDER 64")
    assert errors(mcu) == 1

def test_mclk_source_modclk_accepted(self, mcu):
    # SLAU367P §3.3.2 (CSCTL2.SELM): MODCLK is encoding 4.
    mcu.process("CLOCK:MCLK:SOURCE MODCLK")

# LFMODCLK is MODCLK divided by 128 (SLAU367P §3.2.5).
MODCLK_FREQUENCY_HZ = 4.8e6

Notice that LFMODCLK_FREQUENCY_HZ is computed from MODCLK_FREQUENCY_HZ rather than written as a second literal 37500.0. Same principle as the tree itself: LFMODCLK is MODCLK/128 — encoding the relationship, not the result, means the two constants can never drift apart.

Why VLO and MODCLK are "about" their frequencies

VLO (the very-low-power oscillator) and MODCLK are uncalibrated RC oscillators. The datasheet quotes them as typical values with wide tolerances — VLO can legitimately sit anywhere around 9.4 kHz and wanders with temperature and supply. The simulator models the typical value; the lesson for firmware is that anything timed from VLO is approximate by design (it exists to keep watchdogs and wakeups alive cheaply, not to timestamp anything).

The HFXT honesty comment

HFXT gets a different treatment, and the commit documents why:

# HFXT has no fixed nominal in hardware — it is an external crystal whose
# range is configured via CSCTL4.HFFREQ (SLAU367P §3.3.4, not modeled).
# This is a simulator-only default so HFXT-sourced clocks resolve to a
# concrete frequency.
hfxt_frequency: float = 4e6  # Hz

There is no "typical HFXT frequency" to model — the board designer chooses the crystal. The model needs some value so an HFXT-sourced clock can answer a query, so it picks 4 MHz and labels it a simulator-only default rather than pretending it is a hardware fact. Compare VeREF+ from lesson 0009: board-supplied values get modeled as declared state, not invented constants.

All three FREQUENCY? handlers compute _clock_source_frequency(source) / div and format with f"{freq:.0f}". That format specifier rounds to the nearest integer (Python rounds exact halves to the even neighbour) — unlike the ADC path from lesson 0009, which truncates with int(). Keep the two behaviours straight.

  = lfxt_frequency / mclk_div = 32768 / 1
  → "32768"          # the OLD model answered "1000000" — DCO/1, a 30.5× lie

  → f"{4687.5:.0f}" → "4688"   # .0f rounds; 4687.5 → 4688 (ties-to-even)

Real clock trees produce non-integer frequencies all the time — the SCPI response is a rounded report of a fractional physical rate. Any test asserting 4687 (expecting truncation) fails: this handler is not int().

6. Why This Matters for SIL Testing — the Lying-Frequency Bug Class

A frequency query that ignores the selected source doesn't fail — it answers confidently with the wrong number. Everything downstream that trusts the number inherits the lie.

Downstream victim 1: timer intervals

Timers divide SMCLK or ACLK. Firmware that switches ACLK to VLO for a low-power heartbeat expects ticks at ~9.4 kHz. The old model ticked such timers at 32 768 Hz (LFXT, hardwired), so a "1-second" watchdog pet interval simulated as ~0.29 s. A SIL test around that timing passed in simulation and starved the watchdog on silicon — or vice versa.

Downstream victim 2: UART baud math

On the real FR5994, the eUSCI_A baud-rate generator divides SMCLK (or ACLK). Firmware computes the divisor from the clock frequency it believes it has:

/* firmware under test — BUG: SMCLK was switched to VLO to save power,
   but the baud divisor still assumes the 1-MHz DCO */
select_smclk_source(VLO);                /* CSCTL2.SELS = VLOCLK      */
UCA0BRW = 1000000 / 9600;                /* = 104 — for a 1-MHz clock */
/* actual baud = 9400 / 104 ≈ 90 baud, not 9600 — a ~106× error       */
  • Old model: a SIL script asking CLOCK:SMCLK:FREQUENCY? to cross-check the firmware's assumption got 1000000 back — the same wrong number the firmware assumed. Simulator and bug agreed; the test passed.
  • New model: the query returns 9400. Any assertion tying baud to the reported SMCLK now fails loudly in simulation, where it is cheap to fix.

The pattern: derived-value queries must derive

This is the same disease lesson 0009 diagnosed in the ADC (a hardcoded 3.3-V reference) wearing a different peripheral: a query for a derived value answered from the wrong input. The cure is always the same shape — resolve the configuration chain at read time:

answer(query) = f(current configuration) never f(default configuration), never a cached snapshot — the resolver walks source → base frequency → divider on every call

Why resolve at read time, not at write time?

One could imagine computing the frequency when the source is selected and storing it. That breaks in three ways, all live in this codebase:

  • CLOCK:DCO:FREQUENCY 8e6 after selecting DCO must change what MCLK reports — a snapshot taken at selection time would not.
  • Dividers change independently of sources; two writers to one cached value.
  • The CORNER fault profile's DCO drift is applied inside _dco_actual() at query time; a cache would freeze the drifted value.
⚠ The general lesson
Stored configuration plus derived answers is one honest architecture; stored answers is a lie generator. When you see a getter that returns state without consulting the selector that governs it, you have found this bug class — grep for sibling getters immediately (here the audit found all three FREQUENCY? handlers plus the timer path in one sweep).

7. Often Confused

ConfusionThe distinction
"MCLK's frequency" as a stored property MCLK has no frequency field — only a source and a divider. The frequency is computed per query: _clock_source_frequency(mclk_source) / mclk_div. Storing it would duplicate derivable truth (the double-store bug class).
Clock (MCLK/SMCLK/ACLK) vs. source (DCO/VLO/…) Sources oscillate; clocks route. DCO is an oscillator you can point MCLK at; "MCLK" names the output of the SELM mux and DIVM divider, whoever feeds it. The old bug was exactly conflating the two: treating MCLK as "the DCO, divided".
MODCLK vs. LFMODCLK One oscillator, two taps. MODCLK is the ~4.8-MHz module oscillator; LFMODCLK is the same oscillator through a fixed /128 → 37.5 kHz. The code encodes the relationship: LFMODCLK_FREQUENCY_HZ = MODCLK_FREQUENCY_HZ / 128.
VLO vs. LFXT Both are "slow clocks" but VLO is an internal, uncalibrated ~9.4-kHz RC oscillator (free, imprecise, no crystal needed) while LFXT is an external 32 768-Hz crystal (precise, costs a part and two pins). 32768/9400 ≈ 3.49 — confusing them skews every derived interval by that factor.
SELM/SELS vs. SELA MCLK and SMCLK share one six-entry source menu; ACLK's menu has only the three low-frequency entries. DCO is a valid answer for CLOCK:SMCLK:SOURCE and a -224 for CLOCK:ACLK:SOURCE — same token, different mux.
-224 vs. -222 in the clock handlers -224 "Illegal parameter value": a token outside the enum (SOURCE REFO, SOURCE BANANA). -222 "Data out of range": a number outside the encodable range (DIVIDER 64). Commit 701853d deliberately moved the divider error from -224 to -222.
:.0f rounding vs. int() truncation The clock FREQUENCY? handlers format with f"{freq:.0f}", which rounds (37500/8 = 4687.5 → "4688"). The ADC code path uses int(), which truncates (2047.5 → 2047). Predicting exact simulator outputs requires knowing which one the path uses.

TIMERA0:INTERVAL? 2350        → ≈ 1.0 s

The tick rate is 2350 Hz, so ~2350 ticks ≈ one second. Before the fix, _timer_tick_frequency hardwired ACLK to lfxt_frequency / aclk_div = 32768 Hz, giving a tick rate of 8192 Hz — every interval computed from it was short by 32768/9400 ≈ 3.49×. A "1-second" heartbeat simulated as ~0.29 s, so firmware tuned against the simulator would run 3.5× slow on real silicon. VLO carries no drift factor (only the DCO branch multiplies by faults.dco_factor()), so 2350 Hz is exact in the NOMINAL and CORNER profiles alike.

Scenario B: A teammate reports "the clock model is broken — I set CLOCK:SMCLK:DIVIDER 64 and the divider query still says 1, but no test crashed." What do you check, and what do you tell them?
Show answer

Check the error queue: SYSTEM:ERROR? (or the test helper errors(mcu)). There will be one queued error: -222, "Illegal divider: 64". Nothing crashed because SCPI devices report bad parameters via the error queue, not exceptions to the client — and rejection deliberately leaves the previous state (smclk_div == 1) untouched, which is why the query still says 1.

Then explain the hardware: CSCTL3.DIVS is a 3-bit field whose defined encodings stop at /32 — /64 has no encoding, so no FR5994 can ever be configured that way (SLAU367P §3.3.3). The pre-fix model accepted 64 (and even 128), which meant SIL tests could bless clock configurations no silicon can express. test_mclk_divider_64_rejected — a strict xfail flipped to a real test by 701853d — pins the rejection. If they need a slower clock, the answer is a slower source (VLO, LFMODCLK) or a peripheral-level divider, exactly like real board bring-up.

Scenario C: You are writing a SIL test to prove firmware recomputes its UART divisor when SMCLK moves from the 1-MHz DCO to MODCLK/4. Using only SCPI clock commands, what sequence drives the scenario, and what must CLOCK:SMCLK:FREQUENCY? report at each step? Why would this test have been impossible to write honestly before 701853d?
Show answer 
CLOCK:SMCLK:FREQUENCY?        → "1000000"   (default: DCO 1e6 / 1)
CLOCK:SMCLK:SOURCE MODCLK     ← SELS = MODCLK (encoding 4)
CLOCK:SMCLK:DIVIDER 4
CLOCK:SMCLK:FREQUENCY?        → "1200000"   (4.8e6 / 4)

The firmware's divisor for 9600 baud must move from 1000000/9600 ≈ 104 to 1200000/9600 = 125 — the test asserts the reprogrammed value against the reported SMCLK. Before 701853d this test was unwritable in two ways: first, CLOCK:SMCLK:SOURCE accepted MODCLK only by accident of being unvalidated (it accepted BANANA too — probe_smclk_source_unvalidated), so the selection asserted nothing; second, FREQUENCY? would have reported 1 MHz/div both before and after the switch, so the assertion "the reported frequency changed" could never pass. A test that cannot observe the thing it verifies is not a test — source-aware queries are what make the clock tree observable.

Vocab 0011 · Silmulator · from issue #20, commit 701853d

Clock Trees & Source-Aware Frequency — Vocabulary

Eight terms behind the source-aware clock system. Each has a definition, a project example from the real code, a usage sentence, and a contrast with the term it's most often confused with.

clock tree clock source multiplexer clock divider VLO MODCLK LFMODCLK DCO derived-value query

Clock tree

sources → muxes → dividers → consumers
Definition
The routing structure that distributes a chip's oscillators to its clock consumers: a set of sources feeding per-clock multiplexers, each followed by a divider, whose outputs (MCLK/SMCLK/ACLK on the FR5994) fan out to CPU, timers, and serial peripherals. A clock's frequency is a path property of this tree — selected source ÷ configured divider — not a stored number.
Project example
ClockState in silmulator/devices/msp430.py stores only tree configuration — mclk_source/mclk_div and siblings, plus base rates for DCO/LFXT/HFXT. Commit 701853d made the queries actually walk the tree: _clk_mclk_freq computes _clock_source_frequency(self.clock.mclk_source) / self.clock.mclk_div where it previously hardwired _dco_actual().
Usage
"Before you trust any timer math, draw the clock tree: which source feeds SMCLK, through what divider, and who consumes it."
Contrast with: oscillator
An oscillator (DCO, VLO, a crystal) generates a frequency; the clock tree routes and scales it. MCLK is not an oscillator — it is a route. The pre-fix bug was exactly this confusion: treating MCLK as "the DCO, divided" instead of "whatever SELM selects, divided."

Clock source multiplexer (SELM / SELS / SELA)

CSCTL2 fields — SLAU367P §3.3.2
Definition
The register fields in CSCTL2 that select which oscillator drives each system clock. SELM (MCLK) and SELS (SMCLK) share a six-entry menu — LFXT, VLO, LFMODCLK, DCO, MODCLK, HFXT — while SELA (ACLK) encodes only the three low-frequency sources. Being register fields, the menus are finite: a source with no encoding cannot be selected on any FR5994.
Project example
Mirrored by two frozensets in msp430.py: VALID_MCLK_SMCLK_SOURCES and VALID_ACLK_SOURCES. The module comment records the FR59xx-specific facts: "REFO and DCOCLKDIV have no encoding on the FR59xx CS; MODCLK and LFMODCLK do." Hence CLOCK:MCLK:SOURCE MODCLK is accepted (SELM encoding 4) and REFO draws ScpiError(-224) — the exact inversion of the pre-701853d behaviour.
Usage
"DCO is a fine SMCLK source but ask ACLK's mux for it and you get -224 — SELA simply has no encoding for the fast oscillators."
Contrast with: the divider fields
The mux picks which oscillator; the divider scales how much of it gets through. Both are needed to answer a frequency query, and they fail differently: an unencodable source token is -224, an unencodable divider value is -222.

Clock divider (DIVM / DIVS / DIVA)

CSCTL3 fields — SLAU367P §3.3.3
Definition
The per-clock frequency scalers in CSCTL3. All three are 3-bit fields sharing one encoding: powers of two from /1 to /32. There is no encoding for /64 or /128 (or any non-power like /7) — the divider is an enumerated register field, not an arithmetic knob.
Project example
VALID_CLOCK_DIVIDERS = frozenset({1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32}) in msp430.py. Commit 701853d shrank MCLK's set from the fictional {…, 64, 128}, added the previously missing validation to SMCLK/ACLK, and moved the rejection code to ScpiError(-222, "Illegal divider: …"). The flipped test test_mclk_divider_64_rejected and the rescored probe (_errors(dev) == 1 and dev.clock.mclk_div == 1) pin both the rejection and the untouched prior state.
Usage
"You can't divide ACLK by 7 — DIVA encodes /1 through /32 in powers of two, so pick a slower source instead."
Contrast with: the Timer_A divider chain (ID × TAIDEX)
The CS dividers are a single field with six power-of-two values. The timer's effective divider is a product of two fields (ID /1-/8 × TAIDEX /1-/8), reaching non-powers like /6 and /40 and topping out at /64. Same principle — accepted values are exactly the reachable encodings — different silicon structure, different set.

VLO

very-low-power oscillator — SLAU367P §3.2.6, ~9.4 kHz typical
Definition
The FR5994's internal, uncalibrated low-frequency RC oscillator: ~9.4 kHz typical, no crystal, no configuration register, minimal current. It exists to keep watchdogs, wakeups, and slow timers alive cheaply in low-power modes; its wide tolerance makes anything timed from it approximate by design.
Project example
VLO_FREQUENCY_HZ = 9400.0 — a module constant, because the real oscillator has no register to model. _clock_source_frequency("VLO") returns it directly, so CLOCK:MCLK:SOURCE VLO plus DIVIDER 4 makes CLOCK:MCLK:FREQUENCY? report 2350 — where the pre-701853d model would have reported the DCO's 250 000.
Usage
"The heartbeat runs from VLO to survive LPM3, so budget the watchdog window for ~9.4 kHz plus its tolerance — never for a crisp 32768."
Contrast with: LFXT
Both are "slow" sources on every mux, but LFXT is an external 32 768-Hz watch crystal — precise, costs a part and two pins — while VLO is free and imprecise. The ratio 32768/9400 ≈ 3.49 is exactly how wrong every ACLK-derived timer interval was when the old model hardwired ACLK to LFXT regardless of a VLO selection.

MODCLK

module oscillator — SLAU367P §3.2.5, ~4.8 MHz typical
Definition
The internal ~4.8-MHz RC oscillator of the FR5994's clock system. Like VLO it is fixed-rate — no configuration register — and quoted as a typical value. It gives peripherals and (via SELM/SELS encoding 4) the system clocks a mid-speed source that needs no crystal and no DCO trimming.
Project example
MODCLK_FREQUENCY_HZ = 4.8e6 in msp430.py. The pre-fix model rejected MODCLK as an MCLK source while accepting the nonexistent REFO; the rewritten audit probe probe_mclk_source_set asserts the correction (MODCLK accepted, REFO rejected), and the strict xfail test_mclk_source_modclk_accepted was flipped to a permanent regression test citing "MODCLK is encoding 4."
Usage
"SMCLK from MODCLK/4 gives you a 1.2-MHz peripheral clock with no crystal and no dependence on DCO trim — CLOCK:SMCLK:FREQUENCY? reports 1200000."
Contrast with: DCO
Both are internal oscillators, but the DCO is tunable (a frequency you configure, modeled with ±3.5% CORNER drift) while MODCLK is a fixed typical rate with no knobs. In the resolver that difference is literal: the DCO branch computes dco_frequency × dco_factor(); the MODCLK branch returns a constant.

Definition
The low-frequency tap of the module oscillator: MODCLK passed through a fixed, non-configurable /128, yielding 4.8 MHz / 128 = 37.5 kHz. Not a separate oscillator — a derived output of the same one, giving the low-frequency muxes (including ACLK's SELA) a crystal-free slow source that is faster and stiffer than VLO.
Project example
LFMODCLK_FREQUENCY_HZ = MODCLK_FREQUENCY_HZ / 128 — deliberately written as the relationship rather than a second literal 37500.0, so the two constants can never disagree. Worked example from the lesson: CLOCK:ACLK:SOURCE LFMODCLK + DIVIDER 8 → 37500/8 = 4687.5 → the :.0f format rounds the reply to 4688.
Usage
"No crystal on this board and VLO is too sloppy — run ACLK from LFMODCLK and you get a 37.5-kHz low-frequency clock tied to the module oscillator."
Contrast with: MODCLK
Same oscillator, two taps: MODCLK is the raw ~4.8-MHz output; LFMODCLK is that output through a hardwired /128. The /128 is inside the source, not one of the CSCTL3 dividers — selecting LFMODCLK and then dividing by 8 stacks a configured /8 on top of the built-in /128.

DCO

digitally controlled oscillator — the tunable, drift-affected source
Definition
The FR5994's trimmed internal oscillator, settable to a menu of nominal frequencies (1/4/8/16 MHz class) and accurate only to its trimming tolerance (±3.5%, SLASE54D). It is the reset-default source for MCLK and SMCLK — which is exactly why a frequency query that "always reads DCO" looks right until the first source switch.
Project example
Modeled as clock.dco_frequency (default 1e6, set via CLOCK:DCO:FREQUENCY) resolved through _dco_actual() = dco_frequency × faults.dco_factor() — NOMINAL ×1.0, CORNER ±3.5%. In _clock_source_frequency() the DCO branch is the only drift-affected one; the pre-701853d bug was that MCLK/SMCLK queries called _dco_actual() unconditionally, whatever source was selected.
Usage
"If your timing budget can't absorb ±3.5%, don't leave SMCLK on the DCO — retime the peripheral onto the crystal, and the CORNER profile will prove the difference."
Contrast with: VLO / MODCLK (fixed internal sources)
The DCO is configurable state with modeled drift; VLO and MODCLK are constants with no registers. Consequence in the tree: switching a clock off the DCO also switches off simulated drift for everything downstream of that clock — a real drift-hardening technique the source-aware model can now demonstrate.

Derived-value query

answer = f(current configuration), computed per read
Definition
A query whose answer is not stored anywhere but computed, at read time, from the configuration chain that governs it. For a clock frequency the chain is: resolve the selected source → look up that source's base rate → apply the divider. The anti-patterns are answering from a default link in the chain (the old "always DCO") or caching the answer when the configuration is written.
Project example
_clock_source_frequency() plus the three _clk_*_freq handlers are the pattern's implementation, and _timer_tick_frequency() chains onto it: timer source → that clock's source → base rate → clock divider → timer divider. Recompute-on-read is what makes CLOCK:DCO:FREQUENCY 8e6, a divider change, or CORNER drift show up in the very next query with no cache invalidation anywhere.
Usage
"FREQUENCY? is a derived-value query — if you find yourself storing its answer in a field, you've just created the double-store bug."
Contrast with: stored-state query
A stored-state query echoes configuration back (CLOCK:MCLK:SOURCE? returns the stored token — one fact, one store). A derived-value query combines several stored facts into an answer. The bug class lives in the gap: the old FREQUENCY? pretended to be derived while actually ignoring half its inputs — stored, echoed, never consulted.
